oil.summary: Crude collapsed on Wednesday in one of the sharpest single-session selloffs of the year. WTI settled near $88.54 (-7.84%) and Brent crashed through $95, finishing around $95.12 (-8.19%), after touching its lowest level since early September. The catalyst was a dramatic political shift: following Tuesday's Democratic midterm sweep, President Trump and VP Vance publicly blamed the Iran war for the party's losses, sending markets racing to price an imminent U.S.-Iran diplomatic settlement and the return of sanctioned Iranian barrels. That risk-off signal dominated a session where EIA data actually showed a 900,000-barrel draw — a figure that would normally be supportive. Refined products were also hammered: RBOB fell 6.83% and Heating Oil dropped 6.95%. On the supply side, Nigeria reported output rising to 3.04 million boepd, New Jersey moved to block Russian diesel imports, and Equinor shut its Visund North Sea platform after an electrical fire, removing 13.2 kboepd — though neither event materially offset the Iran-driven selloff. CME options now price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Trump-Iran deal speculation surged after Democrats swept midterms; Brent shed ~$9/bbl intraday on expectations of returning Iranian supply
EIA reported a 900,000-barrel crude inventory draw for the week ending Oct 30, providing no floor amid dominant macro/political sentiment
Equinor's Visund platform fire removed ~13,200 boepd of North Sea supply; Nigeria raised output to 3.04 million boepd, adding further bearish supply context

gas.summary: Natural gas markets diverged sharply on Wednesday. Henry Hub edged higher to $2.96/MMBtu (+2.31% on the day, +5.15% on the week), finding modest support amid forecasts of a potential polar vortex disruption that could send cold air into Northwest Europe and pressure storage levels. TTF, by contrast, cratered 7.17% to €85.03/MWh — its worst single-session drop in weeks — as Iran-deal optimism spilled over from oil markets, reducing risk of a broader Middle East supply disruption and easing LNG premium. The polar vortex warning from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts adds a key downside risk to European storage draws heading into winter. The Equinor Visund outage removes associated gas alongside crude, a marginal supply tightener for European pipe flows. The UAE is also reportedly weighing a third Hormuz bypass pipeline, underscoring ongoing regional infrastructure diversification.
drivers: TTF fell sharply as Iran deal optimism reduced geopolitical risk premium on European LNG supply
Polar vortex forecast from ECMWF threatens early cold-air intrusion into Northwest Europe, putting gas reserves at risk and supporting Henry Hub
Equinor Visund platform fire halted associated gas output in the Norwegian North Sea; UAE evaluating third Hormuz bypass pipeline adds longer-term supply context

power.summary: The power and carbon picture on Wednesday was one of decoupling. EU EUAs held firm at $85.95/EUA (+0.34%), extending a monthly gain of 6.56% and showing resilience against the broader energy commodity selloff. The carbon market appears to be taking its cue from the U.S. political landscape: Democrats swept the midterm elections, triggering a sharp rally in renewables stocks across Asia and Europe as investors re-priced U.S. clean-energy policy expectations. That political tailwind provided a supportive backdrop for carbon prices. TTF's sharp 7.17% drop is a double-edged input — lower gas costs reduce short-term power generation costs and the incentive to switch from coal, which could modestly weigh on carbon demand, though EUA pricing has not reflected this today. Data flow for this sector is otherwise thin.
drivers: Democratic midterm sweep boosted renewables equities globally and provided a supportive policy backdrop for carbon markets
EU EUAs (+0.34%) held firm and extended monthly gains of 6.56% despite broad energy commodity weakness
TTF's 7.17% single-day drop may reduce gas-to-coal switching incentives, a marginal bearish signal for near-term carbon demand — though not yet reflected in EUA prices
